column4: The exact verb يُرَاءُونَ describes hypocrites rising lazily for prayer in order to be seen by people, the section's central scene of a prayer sustained by its human audience.
The spender acts رِئَاءَ ٱلنَّاسِ, and the dust washed from a smooth rock makes the section's mirror-like surface with no depth concrete: the displayed charity leaves nothing to retain.
Spending wealth رِئَآءَ ٱلنَّاسِ is the same audience-facing act as 107:6, now placed in giving rather than prayer.
Those who leave home boastfully and رِئَآءَ ٱلنَّاسِ stage themselves before people, while the verse closes by placing their deeds within Allah's encompassing sight.
أَرَءَيْتَ ٱلَّذِى يَنْهَىٰ repeats the section's opening call to look and directs it at a man whose true character appears in what he does around prayer.
The prohibited object is عَبْدًا إِذَا صَلَّىٰٓ; this row supplies the praying servant on whom the gaze of 96:9 is fixed.
The repeated interrogative asks whether the praying servant is upon guidance, moving the gaze from the visible prayer scene to the servant's actual moral condition.
The same interrogative sequence asks whether the servant commands reverence, making an otherwise unseen exhortation part of the evidence, as 107:3 does with the missing exhortation to feed.
أَرَءَيْتَ again demands an answer about one who denies and turns away, closely joining the gaze-command to the denial named in 107:1.
أَلَمْ يَعْلَم بِأَنَّ ٱللَّهَ يَرَىٰ names Allah as the decisive viewer after the human being has been summoned to look.
This verse identifies the person beneath the prayer confrontation as a human being who transgresses, preparing the deeper diagnosis that outward conduct reveals.
أَن رَّءَاهُ ٱسْتَغْنَىٰ makes false self-sight the cause of transgression: the person holds a flattering mirror to himself and sees independence.
ٱلَّذِى يَرَىٰكَ حِينَ تَقُومُ identifies the One who sees the Prophet when he rises, replacing the human spectators sought by ostentatious prayer with prayer's true witness.
Allah also sees the Prophet's movement among those prostrating, extending the true gaze through the communal prayer scene.
أَفَرَءَيْتَ ٱلَّذِى تَوَلَّىٰ uses the same attention-demand to expose a person by his turning away rather than by his presented appearance.
The man gives a little and then withholds, an unusually close parallel to the small aid withheld at 107:7 after an outwardly visible religious posture.
The question whether he possesses knowledge of the unseen فَهُوَ يَرَىٰ turns seeing into a challenge to his shallow self-assurance and completes the portrait begun at 53:33.
Those who love to be praised for what they did not do depend on a public image detached from reality, the same gap between the viewers' impression and the person's actual deed.
When seen, the hypocrites' bodies impress, yet they are likened to propped timbers; the verse directly opposes attractive visible form to the lack of depth behind it.
The hypocrites say they believe when they meet believers and reverse themselves when alone with their devils, a precise case of conduct that exists only before the desired audience.
Allah could show the hypocrites so that the Prophet would know them by their marks, and their tone already discloses them; the verse models the section's gaze through appearance into identity.
The Prophet is told not to let his eyes pass beyond sincere worshippers seeking Allah's face toward worldly adornment, explicitly redirecting sight from surface display to inward aim.
The unknowing observer mistakes restrained poor people for self-sufficient, while an attentive one recognizes them by their marks; it is a concrete lesson in seeing need beneath appearance.
Noah's chiefs say they see only low-status followers and judge them بَادِىَ ٱلرَّأْىِ, at first glance, embodying the shallow gaze the section rejects.
A man's speech about worldly life pleases the listener and he invokes Allah concerning his heart, yet Allah identifies him as the fiercest adversary; polished presentation hides his reality.
When that pleasing speaker turns away, his movement through the land exposes corruption and destruction; deed supplies the visible finger pointing to what the man is.
A mosque is built for harm and division while its builders swear that they intended only good; a conspicuously religious form functions as a false surface over its purpose.
Qarun comes out before his people in his adornment and awakens the desire of worldly spectators, a full scene of a person presenting a glittering image for others to see.
The command to act says Allah, His Messenger, and the believers will see the deeds, then invokes the Knower of unseen and seen; it names both public witnesses and the gaze that reaches beyond them.
They hide from people but cannot hide from Allah, who is with them during their secret plotting; this exactly reverses the show-off's calculation of when an act has an audience.
Allah knows the stealthy glance of the eyes and what breasts conceal, explicitly carrying sight past the visible eye into hidden intention.
The verse says blindness belongs not to the eyes but to the hearts within breasts, matching the section's distinction between optical seeing and insight into what a person is.
People know only the outward aspect of worldly life while remaining heedless of the Hereafter, a direct statement of the surface-bound gaze opposed by the section.
The command not to declare yourselves pure because Allah best knows the reverent blocks the flattering image a person presents of himself and assigns the deeper judgment to Allah.
أَلَمْ تَرَ إِلَى ٱلَّذِينَ يُزَكُّونَ أَنفُسَهُم asks the listener to look at people who present themselves as pure, then transfers the authority to purify to Allah.
أَرَءَيْتَ مَنِ ٱتَّخَذَ إِلَٰهَهُۥ هَوَىٰهُ directs sight beyond a person's exterior to the desire that actually rules him.
أَفَرَءَيْتَ again exposes desire as a person's real god, then names the sealed heart and veiled sight; it joins commanded scrutiny to failed inward perception.
The one whose evil deed is beautified to him فَرَءَاهُ حَسَنًا mistakes a reflected image of goodness for the deed's truth, a close self-directed form of the section's shallow gaze.
The human being is a witness with insight against himself even while offering excuses, so self-presentation cannot erase the deeper testimony the section asks the hearer to reach.
Whoever does an atom's weight of good يَرَهُ makes even the tiniest deed an eventual object of sight, answering the hidden small kindness at the section's close.
Whoever does an atom's weight of evil يَرَهُ brings an unseen petty refusal under a gaze from which its smallness cannot hide it.
A mustard-seed weight hidden in a rock, heaven, or earth is brought forth by Allah; the verse makes the section's unnoticed small act fully visible to its true knower.

The same passage that next names ostentatious spending first exposes those who are stingy, urge others to stinginess, and conceal Allah's bounty, closely pairing hidden withholding with public display.
The hypocrites come to prayer only lazily and spend only unwillingly, so two visible devotions disclose an inward refusal rather than cover it.
The rebuke that they do not honor the orphan identifies moral reality through treatment of the vulnerable, as the pointing gesture of 107:2 identifies the denier.
They do not urge one another to feed the poor, the exact kind of absent and easily unseen exhortation that the section says must also be noticed.
The condemned person did not urge feeding the poor; this repeated negative act confirms that an omission no crowd notices can reveal the denier.
The people of the Fire confess that they were not among those who prayed, placing the reality of prayer under final disclosure rather than present appearance.
Their next confession is that they did not feed the poor, joining prayer and care for the needy in the same diagnostic sequence as surah 107.
Their confession that they denied the Day of Judgment supplies the hidden denial that the failures of prayer and feeding reveal.
The hypocrites publicly testify to the Messenger while Allah testifies that they lie; the verse sets a polished declaration before the observer who knows its absent depth.
Feeding the poor, orphan, and captive supplies the enacted care missing from surah 107 and is the deed whose unseen motive is voiced in the next ayah.
The givers feed only for Allah's face and seek neither recompense nor thanks, the explicit opposite of acting so that people will look and respond.
The giver offers wealth to purify himself, providing the charitable action whose inward direction 92:19-20 then distinguishes from social exchange and display.
No one's prior favor is being repaid, removing a human audience or social debt as the explanation of the gift.
Seeking only the face of the Most High Lord directs the act toward the opposite gaze from the one sought by ostentation.
Spending to seek Allah's pleasure and to make the self firm is the inwardly rooted counterpart to the rain-stripped ostentatious rock of 2:264.
The verse approves disclosed charity yet calls concealed giving to the poor better, setting a boundary: visibility itself does not make a deed ostentation, and hidden good has a real recipient.
Spending is directed to seeking Allah's face and every good expenditure returns to the giver, opposing the act aimed at people's eyes.
Those who spend by night and day, secretly and openly, receive their reward; the public or hidden setting does not determine sincerity by itself.
Seeking the Lord's face, establishing prayer, and spending secretly and openly appear together, providing a compact inverse of public prayer joined to hidden withholding.
A gift meant to increase within people's wealth does not increase with Allah, whereas alms seeking Allah's face does; the verse separates human-facing appearance from divine value.
Righteousness is not exhausted by turning faces in a ritual direction but includes belief, giving to orphans and the needy, and prayer, a direct boundary between religious surface and substance.
The Prophet is forbidden to stand in the harmful mosque and directed to one founded on reverence, distinguishing two outwardly similar prayer settings by their foundations.
People given knowledge answer Qarun's dazzled spectators that Allah's reward is better, placing a discerning gaze beside the gaze captured by adornment.
The former spectators revise their judgment after Qarun's fall and recognize Allah's apportionment, showing a surface-bound gaze corrected by what the display concealed.
Noah refuses to say that those whom the chiefs' eyes despise will receive no good from Allah, explicitly denying that visible social appearance discloses divine worth.
The Prophet must not drive away socially slighted worshippers who call on their Lord seeking His face; their unseen aim outweighs an audience's status judgment.
Sacrificial meat and blood do not reach Allah, but reverence does, drawing a precise boundary between a ritual's visible material and what gives it value.
Sincere worship directed exclusively to Allah is joined to prayer and almsgiving, the integrated opposite of prayer performed for people while aid is withheld.
The declaration that prayer, sacrifice, life, and death belong to Allah gives prayer the opposite intended recipient from the human gaze sought in showing off.
The praying are excepted from the human tendency to withhold, beginning a direct reversal of the worshippers in surah 107.
Their constancy in prayer contrasts with a prayer dependent on whether people are present to see it.
A recognized right in their wealth prevents prayer from becoming a public surface over private withholding.
That right belongs to the asker and the deprived, completing the inverse relation between genuine prayer and care for those in need.
The command not to oppress the orphan directly reverses the hand that pushes the orphan away in 107:2.
The command not to rebuff the petitioner reverses the unnoticed refusal of small help with which the section ends.
Feeding on a day of hunger supplies active care where the denier's failure to encourage feeding was invisible.
The recipient is an orphan of kin, sharpening the reversal of pushing an orphan away.
The second recipient is a poor person in misery, completing the reversal of withholding food and small aid.
Believing servants are told to establish prayer and spend secretly and openly, a boundary against treating public visibility as proof of insincerity while joining prayer to giving.
Recitation, prayer, and spending secretly and openly form one faithful practice, contrasting with the split between conspicuous prayer and concealed refusal.
Whether good is disclosed or concealed, it remains good; this sets the section's needed boundary between being visible and being performed for visibility.
The Prophet is told not to extend his eyes toward the flower of worldly provision given to others; commanded sight is withdrawn from display and redirected to the Lord's provision.
The Prophet is told not to extend his eyes toward what worldly groups have been given and instead to lower his wing to believers, reversing the spectators' attraction to outward display.
Trust in the Mighty, Merciful One introduces 26:218-219, so dependence is placed on the true viewer rather than on the response of human spectators.
Return is to the Lord, correcting the self-sufficient image of 96:7 and grounding the later reminder that Allah sees.
Some people say publicly that they believe while the verse denies that inward reality, a direct verbal version of the gap between shown form and actual identity.
Their attempt to deceive Allah and believers deceives only themselves, showing that managing human perception cannot manage the true observer.
When challenged over corruption they present themselves as reformers, another attractive public description detached from the action beneath it.
Allah identifies those self-described reformers as corrupters who do not perceive, supplying the deeper judgment their own mirror cannot give.
They profess belief when meeting believers but bite their fingertips when alone, a second concrete instance of conduct changing with the available audience.
The hypocrites use their oaths as a shield, turning visible pious speech into an instrument that hides and protects the contrary deed.
They say with their mouths what is not in their hearts, locating the section's surface-depth split between a publicly available form and a hidden reality.
The laggards say with their tongues what is not in their hearts, another specific outward performance exposed by the speaker who knows its interior.
The question why believers say what they do not do forces the hearer to inspect the distance between presented speech and action.
Allah's hatred of saying what is not done supplies the divine valuation concealed by the speaker's public words.
The question whether to identify the greatest losers by deeds resembles the section's attention-call to inspect a person's true condition through action.
Their effort is lost while they think they are doing well, a self-reflection that looks good to its maker while lacking the reality he attributes to it.
The mirage looks like water to the thirsty but yields nothing when reached, an indirect yet concrete Quranic analogue for the section's image-bearing surface with no depth behind it.
أَفَرَءَيْتَ summons attention to a disbeliever who confidently advertises future wealth and children, exposing a person through the claim he presents.
The reply asks whether he has looked into the unseen or received a covenant, challenging the depth and warrant of the image projected in 19:77.
Insights have come from the Lord, and whoever truly perceives does so for himself; the verse supports the section's movement from eyesight to inward perception.
The earth swallowing Qarun and his adornment reveals how little substance or protection stood behind the public image staged in 28:79.
Worldly life is described as adornment and mutual boasting before its growth withers, making public display a surface whose apparent value cannot endure.
Luqman joins prayer to commanding right and patient action immediately after the hidden mustard-seed image, showing worship operating when no human eye supplies its value.
The ban on turning one's cheek from people and walking boastfully addresses the body as a public pose, the same outward bearing named in the section's dictionary image.
The person neither affirmed nor prayed, beginning another sequence in which denial, prayer, and publicly legible bodily conduct expose one character.
He instead denied and turned away, closely echoing the denial and turning scrutinized in 96:13 and the denier identified in 107:1.
He then goes to his people swaggering, giving denial an outward posture presented before his social circle.
The verse contrasts one on clear proof with people whose evil deeds are beautified to them and who follow desire, linking false self-sight to the reality it conceals.
A person reads abundant provision as proof that his Lord has honored him, judging his own worth by the visible surface of wealth before 89:17 corrects him.
He reads restricted provision as humiliation, another shallow self-judgment overturned by the following exposure of how he treats the vulnerable.
Greedily consuming inheritance continues the concrete actions through which the false self-assessment of 89:15-16 is exposed.
Excessive love of wealth names the inward attachment behind the visible failures toward orphan and poor.
Failure to believe in Allah the Great supplies the inward condition paired in the next ayah with the unseen failure to urge feeding the poor.
The question asking what put them in the Fire calls for an account, and the succeeding answers reveal prayer, feeding, and denial as the hidden truth of their lives.
Joining those engaged in empty talk adds the social company before which their conduct occurred, between neglected care and denial of judgment.
The passage diagnoses the human being as anxiously grasping before contrasting that disposition with genuine prayer and a known right for the needy.
Distress makes the person panic, part of the inner portrait whose next movement is withholding when good reaches him.
When good touches him he becomes withholding, the exact disposition from which the consistent worshippers of 70:22 are excepted.
The question asking what can make the hearer know the steep path is another attention-command whose answer comes through costly care rather than displayed form.
Freeing a person from bondage begins the answer to 90:12 with an unambiguously beneficial act before the feeding of orphan and poor.
Even a mustard-seed weight is brought into the just scales, so an apparently negligible hidden refusal cannot remain outside judgment.
Whether what is in breasts is concealed or disclosed, Allah knows it, directly placing inner purpose beyond the performer's control of appearances.
No private conversation escapes Allah's presence and eventual disclosure, extending the true audience into precisely the setting where people suppose no one sees.
Guardians stand over human beings even when no human spectator is present, challenging the premise that an unseen act has no witness.
The guardians are noble recorders, giving the hidden deed a durable account rather than the passing image sought from people.
They know what people do, completing the alternative audience introduced in 82:10.
Two offerings are outwardly comparable, but acceptance belongs only to the reverent; the result depends on a reality beneath the performed rite.
Hypocrites enjoin wrong, forbid right, and close their hands, joining a communal religious identity to the withholding action that reveals it as hollow.
Believing allies enjoin right, establish prayer, and give alms, providing the integrated social action absent from the showy worshipper's public image.
They swear to people in order to please them, while Allah and His Messenger are more entitled to be pleased; the verse identifies a misdirected audience and corrects it.
Fearing people's reaction while Allah has greater right to be feared is a specific boundary between action governed by human eyes and action governed by the true observer.
More indirectly, criminals see the believers and declare them astray; their confident human gaze supplies a concrete instance of spectators judging persons without access to their truth.
The Last Day reverses the spectatorship as believers laugh at the disbelievers, though the link to ostentatious worship is indirect and depends on the neighboring gaze scenes.
The believers are seated looking on, completing the reversal of 83:32; it illuminates the fallibility of the earlier human audience rather than showing off itself.
The frown is a visible facial act whose moral meaning Allah calls the addressee to inspect, closely matching the section's way of identifying a person through a small movement.
The occasion is the arrival of a blind man, making physical sight and the failure to perceive a person's worth part of the same scene.
The question raises the visitor's unseen possibility of purification, directing judgment beyond what his outward status disclosed.
The visitor might receive a reminder that benefits him, naming an inward effect unavailable to the shallow social appraisal that first dismissed him.
Attention turns toward the person who presents himself as self-sufficient, recalling the false self-sight of 96:7 and the section's attractive surface.
The addressee gives the self-sufficient man attentive reception, staging the human gaze as a scarce good directed by visible rank.
The addressee is not accountable for that man's refusal to purify himself, correcting the social calculation that made him the preferred spectator.
The sincere seeker comes eagerly, so his movement provides the evidence of character that social appearance had obscured.
The blind seeker's inward fear is the reality beneath his unimportant outward standing.
Turning attention away from the sincere seeker completes a scene in which the commanded gaze must be corrected from prestige to inward receptivity.
People ask contemptuously whether these are the ones Allah favored among them; Allah's knowledge of the grateful corrects their status-bound gaze at the worshippers of 6:52.
Noah refuses to drive away the lowly believers because they will meet their Lord and tells the chiefs he sees them acting ignorantly, countering their first-glance judgment in 11:27.
Noah's people reject belief because low-status people follow him, a repeated scene in which observers mistake social appearance for spiritual identity.
Noah asks what knowledge he has of the followers' deeds, marking the limit of a human observer's access to their true account.
He assigns their accounting to his Lord, transferring final knowledge from the disdainful spectators to the true judge.
He refuses to drive believers away, acting on the deeper appraisal rather than the crowd's surface valuation.

The two mosques are distinguished by foundations: reverence and divine pleasure versus the crumbling edge of a precipice, giving architectural depth to the contrast between identical religious surfaces.
The false building remains a source of doubt within its builders' hearts, explicitly joining the displayed structure to the concealed interior named in 9:107.
Qarun claims his wealth came from knowledge he possessed, a flattering self-image that prepares his public appearance in adornment and ignores Allah's deeper knowledge of prior destroyers.
They covenant that if Allah gives bounty they will give charity and be righteous, establishing the publicly stated image against which their later withholding is read.
When bounty arrives they become stingy and turn away, so action uncovers the person beneath the earlier promise.
Hypocrisy in their hearts results from breaking the promise and lying, explicitly locating the inward reality produced by the outward sequence.
The closing question asks whether they know Allah knows their secret and private counsel, naming the true viewer of what their public promise concealed.
The one who is stingy and considers himself self-sufficient joins concealed withholding to the same false self-appraisal depicted in 96:7.
His denial of the best names the inward rejection disclosed through the stinginess of 92:8.
Being eased toward hardship reveals the actual direction hidden beneath his self-sufficient image.
If people were pressed for their wealth they would become stingy and Allah would expose their resentments, directly making withholding a disclosure of the heart.
The hearers are called to spend, but some withhold; the verse says stinginess harms the self while Allah remains rich, correcting the withholder's self-interested calculation.
When told to spend from Allah's provision, the disbelievers answer that Allah could feed the needy Himself; their spoken refusal makes denial visible through failure to feed.
The hypocrites privately command others not to spend on those with the Messenger so that they disperse, a hidden exhortation to withhold that exposes the reality behind their public testimony.
The rebuke to people who command righteousness of others while forgetting themselves exposes a public religious voice whose own action has no matching depth.
They say obedience in the Prophet's presence, then a group plots at night to the contrary while Allah records it, an exact audience-dependent reversal between shown and hidden conduct.
A group professes belief when meeting believers but challenges one another when alone, repeating the section's scene of behavior calibrated to who is looking.
The question reminds them that Allah knows what they conceal and disclose, placing both performances before the viewer they omitted from their calculation.
Some say they believe with their mouths although their hearts do not believe; the Messenger is told not to grieve over this explicit surface-depth split.
No deed is begun without Allah witnessing it, and not even an atom's weight is hidden from Him; the verse unites the true spectator with the section's smallest unnoticed act.
Joseph's brothers present his shirt with false blood, but Jacob rejects the staged evidence and diagnoses what their selves enticed them to do, a concrete false image read past its surface.
The Lord is described as being on watch immediately before the human being misreads wealth as honor and his treatment of orphan and poor is exposed.

Clothing provides visible covering and adornment, while the garment of reverence is declared better; the verse directly distinguishes a person's dress from the deeper quality the section asks one to see.
The ban on ridicule warns that those socially belittled may be better than their mockers, setting an explicit limit on judgments made from public appearance.
Tribal and social differences make people recognizable, but honor before Allah is measured by reverence known to Him, separating visible identity from actual worth.
The ban on walking exultantly rejects the body used as a public display of importance and recalls that such posture cannot give the person the greatness it advertises.
The servants of the Merciful walk humbly and answer ignorance peacefully, providing an outward bearing whose visible form expresses rather than masks inward allegiance.
Moderation in walking and lowering the voice correct the boastful public posture forbidden in 31:18 and gives bodily presentation a truthful measure.
The one who gives and is reverent opens the opposite path from the stingy, self-sufficient person of 92:8.
Affirming the best names the inward conviction expressed through the giver's action.
Being eased toward ease discloses the giver's true direction, against the hardship hidden beneath the withholder's self-image.
The successful believers are inwardly humble in prayer, supplying the opposite interior to prayer performed for watching people.
Their active concern with purification or almsgiving joins prayer to giving rather than to withholding.
Those who answer their Lord establish prayer, conduct affairs by consultation, and spend from provision; responsive worship and social giving form one life rather than a displayed ritual shell.

Trade does not distract these people from remembrance, prayer, and almsgiving because they fear a Day on which hearts and eyes overturn; their worship is governed by the final gaze rather than the market's audience.
The righteous sleep little at night, placing worship in a setting largely unavailable to human spectators.
They seek forgiveness before dawn, continuing the private devotion that precedes their provision for the needy.
Their wealth contains a right for the asker and deprived, joining unseen worship to material care in the direct reverse of surah 107's split.
Their sides leave their beds to call upon their Lord in fear and hope, and they spend from His provision; private prayer and giving are united in one ayah.
No soul knows the hidden joy reserved for those deeds, so the unseen act receives an unseen reward beyond any spectators' response.
Establishing prayer, giving alms, and certainty in the Hereafter appear together, reversing the denial, showy prayer, and withholding linked in surah 107.
Prayer is said to restrain indecency and wrongdoing, giving genuine prayer a moral effect beyond the visible performance criticized in the section.
Belief in the unseen, prayer, and spending from provision are joined, placing worship and giving under an orientation deeper than human sight.
Prayer and almsgiving are followed by the assurance that whatever good is sent ahead will be found with Allah, who sees what people do; value rests with the true viewer.
The true believers establish prayer and spend from provision after their hearts respond to Allah's mention, explicitly joining inward state, worship, and giving.
Humble hearts, patience, prayer, and spending are listed together, providing an integrated piety opposite to an impressive prayer surface over a closed hand.
The one hoping to meet the Lord must do righteous work and associate no one in worship, a direct boundary against making human spectators partners in a devotional act.
The command to worship Allah with religion made sincere for Him gives devotion the exclusive orientation denied by ostentation.
The speaker is commanded to worship Allah sincerely, again locating worship's intended recipient beyond human eyes.
The declaration of worship sincerely for Allah alone makes the reversal of audience explicit.
A provisioned person spends secretly and openly in the parable, reinforcing that visibility is a circumstance of giving rather than proof that it is done to be seen.
Those who spend and do not follow the gift with reminders or injury preserve the recipient's good, opposing charity used to construct the giver's public image.
A kind word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by hurt, placing the needy person's treatment above the visible fact of giving just before 2:264 names ostentation.
Disbelievers dismiss revelation because socially disfavored people reached it before them, a specific status-bound gaze that treats audience rank as a measure of truth.
Qarun's heavy treasures and exultation begin the public-image scene before his adorned appearance, and the warning not to exult already challenges his posture.
He is told to seek the Hereafter, do good, and avoid corruption with what Allah gave him, supplying the unrealized inward use against which his later display is judged.
Those who withhold Allah's bounty think the act good for them, but it will become a visible collar, turning concealed stinginess into disclosed judgment.
The verse repeats the portrait of people who are stingy and command others to stinginess, extending the section's concern from a withheld object to a hidden social influence.
Whatever people spend or vow is known by Allah, assigning the evaluation of giving to a witness beyond the giver's managed audience.
Not even an atom's weight in heaven or earth is hidden from the Knower of the unseen, so small concealed conduct remains within the true field of vision.
Whether speech is concealed or voiced aloud, Allah knows what breasts contain, directly joining presentation and intention under one knowledge.
The Creator's subtle awareness grounds the preceding claim that hidden speech and hearts cannot escape Him.
Allah knows what people conceal and disclose and what breasts contain, a repeated formulation of the depth unavailable to the human audience.
People return to forbidden private counsels and speak of sin while supposing secrecy, giving the divine presence named in 58:7 a concrete hidden action to observe.
Some hypocrites are unknown even to the Prophet while Allah knows them, a needed boundary on the human gaze summoned by the section.
Worldly life is beautified for disbelievers who mock believers, but the reverent will be above them at resurrection; present spectatorship and final worth diverge.
The Prophet is told not to be impressed by wealth and children, explicitly refusing visible abundance as evidence of a person's favored reality.
The Prophet is told not to be deceived by the disbelievers' movement through the lands, redirecting judgment away from their publicly visible success.
That visible success is only brief enjoyment before a wretched destination, supplying the concealed depth beneath the movement of 3:196.
Wealth and children are the adornment of worldly life, while enduring righteous deeds are better with the Lord, distinguishing displayed assets from lasting moral substance.
Worldly provision and adornment are set against what is with Allah as better and more lasting, another boundary between an attractive visible image and actual value.
They swear publicly that they belong with the believers although the verse denies it, making an oath the surface of a frightened contrary identity.
Their readiness to flee into any refuge reveals the fear beneath the belonging they displayed in 9:56.
